statement: A lunch is soup or salad, then fish or rice, then cake or fruit. Lucy picks one from each pair. How many different lunches can she pick?

choices.misconception: I counted one choice for each of the three parts of the lunch.
I stopped my tree after the first two parts and forgot the cake or fruit.
I added 2 + 2 + 2 instead of letting every choice branch out again.
I tried to list them all without a tree and missed one lunch, salad with rice and fruit.

hints: Draw a tree that starts with soup or salad.
A tree diagram has a branch for each first choice, then from every one of those a branch for each second choice, and again for the third. Count the ends of the last branches.
Soup or salad gives 2 branches. Each splits into fish or rice, giving 4. Each of those splits into cake or fruit.

solutions.reliable: Starting with soup: soup-fish-cake, soup-fish-fruit, soup-rice-cake, soup-rice-fruit. That is 4 lunches. Salad gives the same 4 with salad instead of soup. In all 4 + 4 = 8 lunches. The idea to keep: a tree keeps a list complete, because every branch splits the same way.
solutions.elegant: Each part doubles the number of lunches: 2 after the first part, 4 after the second, 8 after the third. The idea to keep: every new two-way choice doubles the count.

whyOnTest: A three-step choice is where adding instead of branching goes wrong, and a tree shows why.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
